how-i-set-up-9router-with-claude-code-fo.title: How I Set Up 9router with Claude Code for Seamless AI Coding Across Devices
how-i-set-up-9router-with-claude-code-fo.content:
I code on multiple machines. A Mac Mini that sits at home running 24/7, a MacBook Pro that travels with me everywhere, and occasionally a Windows PC. Each one needs access to AI coding tools, and managing API keys, model providers, and configurations across all of them was becoming a headache.

That is, until I put together a setup with 9router, Claude Code, and a handy little tool called CCC. Let me walk you through how I made it all work.

## The Problem

Here is what I was dealing with:

- I use Claude Code daily for coding. It needs a provider endpoint and API key configured.
- I have multiple AI model providers I want to use. Some go through 9router, some are direct like Anthropic or Z.AI for GLM models.
- My MacBook already runs of local projects. Running an AI router on top of that eats CPU and memory.
- When I travel, I need access to the same AI tools without fiddling with configs.

The core issue: I needed one consistent setup that works everywhere, without wasting resources on my laptop.

## What is 9router?

9router is an OpenAI-compatible API gateway. You point your AI tools at it, and it routes requests to whatever model provider you have configured behind the scenes. Think of it as a middleman that lets you swap providers without touching your app configs.

It comes with a dashboard where you can see usage analytics, manage API keys, and configure endpoints. The key feature for me is that I configure it once and everything behind it just works.

## The Architecture I Landed On

After some trial and error, here is what I ended up with:

**Mac Mini (home server)** runs 9router locally on port 20128. It is always on, always reachable on the home network.

**A VPS** runs another instance of 9router via Docker in Easypanel. This is my fallback for when I am not at home.

**Anthropic** for direct access to Claude models without going through 9router.

**Z.AI** for direct access to GLM models without going through 9router.

My MacBook just connects to whichever endpoint makes sense at the moment. At home, it hits the Mac Mini directly. On the road, it falls back to the VPS.

## Why Not Just Run Everything on the MacBook?

I tried that. The problem is that 9router adds overhead. When you are already running multiple dev servers, Docker containers, and who knows what else on a laptop, adding an API gateway on top is just unnecessary weight.

The Mac Mini sits there doing nothing most of the time anyway. Might as well put it to work.

## Why the VPS Fallback?

Because I travel a lot. My MacBook goes everywhere with me, and I cannot always be on my home network.

I tested a few options for remote access:

| Route | Latency |
|-------|---------|
| Mac Mini local | ~5ms |
| VPS with Cloudflare proxy | ~83ms |
| Mac Mini via tunnel | ~842ms |

The VPS route won. 83ms overhead on an AI request that already takes seconds to respond is barely noticeable. The tunnel was way too slow at nearly a second of overhead.

## Making it Easy to Switch: CCC

Here is where it gets good. Nobody wants to manually edit config files every time they switch networks.

I found this tool called [CCC (Claude Code Config Switcher)](https://github.com/guyskk/claude-code-config-switcher). It lets you define multiple provider profiles and switch between them with a single command.

You install it, create a config at `~/.claude/ccc.json`, and define your providers:

```json
{
  "providers": {
    "home": {
      "env": {
        "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "http://localhost:20128/v1",
        "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": "your-api-key",
        "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL": "coding",
        "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "pro",
        "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL": "deepseek"
      }
    },
    "cloud": {
      "env": {
        "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "https://your-vps-domain.com/v1",
        "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": "your-api-key",
        "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL": "coding",
        "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "pro",
        "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL": "deepseek"
      }
    },
    "zai": {
      "env": {
        "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "https://api.z.ai/api/anthropic",
        "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": "your-api-key",
        "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL": "glm-5.1",
        "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "glm-4.7"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Then to switch providers, I just run:

```bash
ccc home    # Mac Mini, fastest
ccc cloud   # VPS, when traveling
ccc zai     # Direct Z.AI for GLM models
```

One command, no config editing, no restarting. It just works.

The important thing here is that you need to remove the `ANTHROPIC_*` env vars from your `~/.claude/settings.json` file. CCC manages those now. If you leave them in `settings.json`, they will conflict and override what CCC tries to set. The tool actually catches this and warns you, which is nice.

## The Mac Mini Hostname Trick

One small but useful thing: instead of remembering the Mac Mini's local IP address (which can change), I renamed its hostname to `macmini.local` using Bonjour. Now the MacBook can always reach it at `http://macmini.local:20128/v1` regardless of what IP the router assigns.

On macOS it is just three commands:

```bash
sudo scutil --set ComputerName macmini
sudo scutil --set LocalHostName macmini
sudo scutil --set HostName macmini
```

No restart needed. Takes effect immediately.

## Adding the Provider to My Statusline

I like seeing which provider I am currently using at a glance. I added it to my Claude Code statusline script. It reads the `current_provider` field from `ccc.json` and displays it alongside the model name, project, duration, and context bar.

Now my statusline looks like this:

```
glm | home | my-project | main | 5m 32s | 60%
```

That little `home` indicator tells me instantly which backend I am hitting.

## What About Cloudflare WARP?

If you use Cloudflare WARP (like I do for work), it might block Bonjour `.local` hostname resolution since WARP routes DNS through Cloudflare instead of your local network.

The good news is that if `macmini.local` does not resolve, I just run `ccc cloud` and hit the VPS instead. It is not as fast, but it works from anywhere. Alternatively, you can configure WARP split tunnel to exclude your home subnet so local traffic stays local.

## The Full Picture

Here is what the setup looks like end to end:

1. **Mac Mini** runs 9router on port 20128, always on, always available at `macmini.local`
2. **VPS** runs 9router in Docker via Easypanel, accessible from anywhere
3. **MacBook** uses CCC to switch between `home` (Mac Mini), `cloud` (VPS), or `zai` (direct GLM)
4. **9Remote** installed on the MacBook for phone access when I am away from a keyboard

All usage analytics and API key management live in one place. No syncing databases between devices. No duplicate configs. Just clean, simple switching.

## Why This Setup Works for Me

- **Performance first.** At home where I do most of my heavy coding, I get near-zero latency hitting the local Mac Mini.
- **Flexibility on the road.** When I travel, one command switches me to the VPS or direct Z.AI access.
- **Resource efficiency.** My MacBook does not waste CPU and memory running an API gateway.
- **Single source of truth.** One 9router instance for analytics, one config to manage.
- **Zero manual config editing.** CCC handles the switching. I just type `ccc home` or `ccc cloud` and start coding.

If you are juggling multiple AI providers and devices like I am, this combination of 9router plus CCC is honestly hard to beat. It took me an afternoon to set up, and it has been running smoothly ever since.

web-storage-localstorage-sessionstorage-.title: Web Storage: localStorage, sessionStorage, and Cookies
web-storage-localstorage-sessionstorage-.content:
When it comes to building cool stuff on the web, managing data is like having superpowers. There are three cool tools - `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, and `cookies` - that help web developers do just that. In this guide, I'll take a peek into what makes each of them special, what they're good at, and where they might stumble a bit.

> localStorage

`localStorage` is a reliable storage option that allows us to store key-value pairs in a user's browser for an extended period.

#### Pros:
- **Persistence**: Data persists even when the user closes and reopens the browser.
- **Ample Storage**: Provides a generous storage space (around 5MB), making it suitable for larger amounts of data.
- **Simplicity**: User-friendly API, making it easy to implement.

#### Cons:
- **Single Domain Limitation**: Data is limited to the domain that created it.
- **Security Concerns**: Vulnerable to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks.

#### Example:
```javascript
// Storing data in localStorage
localStorage.setItem('username', 'JohnDoe');

// Retrieving data from localStorage
const username = localStorage.getItem('username');
console.log(username); // Output: JohnDoe

```

> sessionStorage

`sessionStorage` is similar to localStorage but with a shorter lifespan, suitable for storing data for the duration of a user's visit to a specific page.

#### Pros:
- **Session-Based**: Data is only available for the duration of the page session.
- **Isolation**: Each page/tab gets its own sessionStorage, preventing data conflicts between tabs.
- **No Persistence Overhead**: Data is automatically cleared when the session ends.

#### Cons:
- **Limited Lifespan**: Data is lost when the user closes the tab or browser.
- **Single Domain Limitation**: Similar to localStorage, it is limited to the domain.

#### Example:

```javascript
// Storing data in sessionStorage
sessionStorage.setItem('language', 'JavaScript');

// Retrieving data from sessionStorage
const language = sessionStorage.getItem('language');
console.log(language); // Output: JavaScript

```

> Cookies

`Cookies` are small pieces of data stored on a user's device, accessible by both the server and client.

#### Pros:
- **Cross-Domain Availability**: Can be accessed by different domains, facilitating data sharing.
- **Versatility**: Can store various data types, not just strings.
- **Expiration Control**: Can set expiration times for data.

#### Cons:
- **Size Limitations**: Limited to around 4KB of data per cookie.
- **Performance Overhead**: Adds a bit of overhead to each HTTP request.
- **Security Risks**: Vulnerable to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks.

### Example:
```javascript
// Setting a cookie
document.cookie = 'theme=light; expires=Fri, 31 Dec 2023 23:59:59 GMT; path=/';

// Retrieving cookies
const cookies = document.cookie;
console.log(cookies); // Output: theme=light

```

> Choosing the Right Tool for the Job

#### Factors to Consider:

- **Data Size**: For larger amounts of data, localStorage might be a better fit.
- **Data Lifespan**: If data needs to persist across different pages or tabs, consider localStorage or cookies. For shorter durations, use sessionStorage.
- **Cross-Domain Requirements**: If your application involves data sharing across different domains, cookies are the go-to solution.

introduction-to-nextjs-building-modern-w.title: Introduction to Next.js: Building Modern Web App
introduction-to-nextjs-building-modern-w.content:
In recent years, web development has undergone a significant transformation, with a shift towards building dynamic and interactive applications. With the rise of Single-Page Applications (SPAs) and the demand for better performance and user experiences, developers are constantly seeking tools and frameworks that simplify the process of building robust web applications. Next.js, a popular React framework, has emerged as a powerful solution for building modern web applications with ease.

### **What is Next.js?**

Next.js is an open-source framework for building web applications, created by Vercel (formerly known as Zeit). It is built on top of React and offers a powerful set of features that enable developers to build scalable and production-ready applications. Next.js provides a solution for server-side rendering (SSR) and static site generation (SSG), making it an excellent choice for applications that require fast loading times, SEO optimization, and a great user experience.

### **Key Features of Next.js:**

1. **Server-side rendering (SSR)**: One of the standout features of Next.js is its support for SSR. Unlike traditional client-side rendering, where the HTML is generated by the browser, SSR allows you to pre-render pages on the server and send them to the client already populated with data. This approach improves performance and ensures that search engines can easily index your content.
2. **Static site generation (SSG)**: Next.js also supports SSG, which allows you to pre-render static pages at build time. This means that your application can benefit from the performance gains of serving static files, while still being able to fetch data dynamically when needed. SSG is particularly useful for content-driven websites or blogs.
3. **Automatic code splitting**: Next.js optimizes your application's performance by automatically splitting your JavaScript code into smaller chunks. Only the code necessary for each page is loaded, resulting in faster initial page loads and improved user experience. Additionally, Next.js optimizes assets for delivery, such as images and CSS, making your application even more efficient.
4. **API routes**: Next.js provides a built-in API routes feature that allows you to create serverless functions to handle server-side logic. This makes it easy to create custom APIs or backend functionality within your Next.js application, without the need for an additional server.
5. **CSS support**: Next.js offers various options for styling your applications, including CSS modules, styled-jsx, and support for popular CSS-in-JS libraries like styled-components and Tailwind CSS. This flexibility allows you to choose the styling approach that best suits your project.
6. **Hot module replacement**: Next.js includes a feature called Hot Module Replacement (HMR), which allows you to update your code in real-time without losing the application's state. This feature significantly speeds up the development process, as you can instantly see the changes reflected in the browser.

### **Getting Started with Next.js:**

To start using Next.js, you'll need to have Node.js and npm (Node Package Manager) installed on your machine. You can then create a new Next.js project by running a simple command in your terminal:

```jsx
npx create-next-app my-app
```

This command will set up a new Next.js project with all the necessary dependencies and a basic folder structure. From there, you can navigate to the project directory and start the development server:

```jsx
cd my-app
npm run dev
```

Next.js will launch a development server and provide you with a local URL where you can access your application. You can then start building your Next.js application by creating pages, components, and leveraging the framework's powerful features.

### **Conclusion:**

Next.js has quickly become a popular choice among developers for building modern web applications. Its support for server-side rendering, static site generation, and automatic code splitting makes it an excellent framework for creating fast, SEO-friendly applications. With its easy setup and integration with React, Next.js empowers developers to focus on building great user experiences while taking advantage of the latest web development techniques. Whether you're building a small personal website or a complex enterprise application, Next.js can be a valuable tool in your web development toolbox.
